name: Niche perfume / sample decants

lead: Decants are small portions of a perfume transferred into a vial so you can wear a fragrance for days before paying for a full bottle. Niche perfumery refers to smaller houses whose scents are positioned apart from mass-market designer releases and are often pricier.

By living with a scent on your own skin, you can judge how it smells on you and whether it fits your style before committing. Encyclopedic coverage of the practice is minimal; it is popular in fragrance communities.

paras: People order a few vials of scents they are curious about, wear each across a few days or occasions, and buy a full bottle only for the one they keep reaching for. It is common to rotate several samples before deciding.
As with any fragrance, ingredients can cause skin allergy or breathing irritation in some people. Source and handling of decants vary by seller, so authenticity and storage are the buyer's to judge.

chain: Find a scent that suits you
angle.text: Small vials let you test expensive niche perfumes on your own skin before buying a full bottle, so you settle on a scent that suits you. You then wear a fragrance that fits your style and presentation.

lead: Decants are small portions of a perfume transferred from a full bottle into a small spray vial, sold so buyers can wear a fragrance for days before committing to a full bottle. "Niche" perfumery refers to smaller houses that use selective distribution and target a narrower audience than mass-market designer releases.[1]

People use decants to build a signature scent, which is part of grooming and how a person is perceived. One retailer, Scento, argues that a brief in-store test misses how a fragrance develops and wears over several days and in different weather, and that decants let buyers sample several scents for the price of one bottle.[2] Its listed sizes are 2, 5 and 8 ml, with roughly 30, 75 and 120 sprays respectively.[2]

Niche perfumery gained a following in Europe and North America in the late 20th and early 21st centuries; Luca Turin and Tania Sanchez call L'Artisan Parfumeur, founded in 1976, the first niche firm.[1] Concentration terms help buyers compare products: parfum or extrait contains roughly 15 to 30 percent aromatic compounds, eau de parfum about 15 percent and eau de toilette 5 to 15 percent, though houses set their own concentrations.[3]

paras: Natural perfume materials come from plants, animals, lichens and seaweed, while synthetics are produced by a small number of large companies.[3] Because scent labels such as eau de parfum are imprecise and can vary between houses, the same name can denote different strengths.[3]

Wikipedia's niche perfume article says niche houses make smaller batches than designer or celebrity fragrances, that the 1995 opening of the New York boutique Aedes de Venustas is cited as the start of a boom, and that luxury conglomerates bought many niche lines in the 2010s, blurring the line with designer brands.[1]

Scento says its decants are hand-filled from sealed bottles obtained from authorised European retailers, and lists advantages including lower upfront spend, more realistic testing over several days, fewer unworn full bottles and easy rotation by mood or season. It also acknowledges that decants usually cost more per millilitre than full bottles and lack the box and presentation of a sealed bottle.[2] These are seller statements; no independent data on authenticity or storage were found.

Fragrance is discussed alongside grooming and style as part of overall presentation, and decants come up as a way to try expensive scents without full-bottle purchases. Specific community sources were not available for citation.
Fragrance ingredients can trigger skin allergies, headaches and asthma reactions in some people.[3] Perfume contents are rarely disclosed in full, as companies cite trade secrets.[3]

timeline.event: L'Artisan Parfumeur is founded; Turin and Sanchez call it the first niche firm.[1]
Aedes de Venustas opens in New York, cited as the start of a niche boom.[1]
Estee Lauder buys Jo Malone London, an early niche acquisition by a luxury group.[1]
